summary: Specifies a transport protocol for RID messages, which carry IODEF incident reports between network operators. It builds on the XML exchange format defined for incident data. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 6546.

eli5.summary: This is the delivery truck for security alert messages that networks send each other. It was replaced by RFC 6546.

subtitle: How Real-time Inter-network Defense messages travel between security teams: plain HTTP POSTs over mutually authenticated TLS.

tldr.problem: Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID) needs an agreed transport so that members of a consortium of network operators can exchange incident messages and interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: RID messages are sent as HTTP POST requests to the path / over TLS with mutual authentication, to TCP port 4590. A receiver can answer at once or reply 202 Accepted and call back later with its own request.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational document, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 6546.

today: RFC 6046 is an Informational document that has been obsoleted by RFC 6546. It was written alongside RFC 6045, which was itself replaced by RFC 6545.

sections.title: Why RID Needs a Transport
sections.content:
The Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF, RFC 5070) defines an XML document format for sharing incident data between security response teams. It deliberately defines a message format and not a transport protocol, so teams can store and exchange messages in whatever way suits them.

Real-time Inter-network Defense (RID, RFC 6045) is different: it needs a transport specification so that all members of a RID consortium can interoperate. This document supplies one, carrying RID messages in HTTP requests and responses over Transport Layer Security (TLS). The text notes that any IODEF message can also be sent this way, by wrapping it as a RID Report message.
sections.eli5: The format for the alert note was already agreed, but nobody had said how to deliver it. This document picks the delivery method.

sections.title: RID over HTTP and TLS
sections.content:
Each RID system plays both roles: it is an HTTP/TLS client when it sends a message and an HTTP/TLS server when it receives one. Every RID system MUST be ready to accept connections from any RID peer it talks to, because delayed replies come back as new connections.

RID systems listen for TCP connections on port 4590, and every participant in a consortium MUST listen there. All RID messages in HTTP requests MUST use POST with a Request-URI of /. Other paths are reserved for future use by RID.

The document admits that HTTP/TLS is not an ideal fit, because HTTP is a client-server protocol while RID is a message-exchange protocol. It concludes that the ease of implementing RID systems over HTTP/TLS outweighs this concern. Systems MUST support HTTP/1.1 persistent connections (and SHOULD use them) and MUST support chunked transfer encoding on the server side.
sections.eli5: Every office both sends and receives mail, so every office must keep one particular door open for deliveries. All packages are handed over the same way.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Callback
sections.content:
A RID system MUST be ready to handle only the response types listed for the request it sent, and MUST NOT answer with any RID message other than the one that corresponds to the request. For example, a TraceRequest may be answered with a RequestAuthorization, a Result, or an empty 202.

Queries and replies can be far apart in time. A receiver MAY therefore answer 202 Accepted with an empty body, close the connection, and later open a new connection to the original sender and send the reply as an HTTP request. This is called RID callback. The callback goes to the network and transport addresses the request came from; there is no mechanism for redirected callback. A system that receives a callback request MUST return 202 Accepted.

If the reply is available immediately or within a generally accepted HTTP client timeout (about thirty seconds), the receiver SHOULD send it in the HTTP response. Senders still MUST be prepared for a 202 and a later callback.

On errors, an improper RID message in a request gets a 4xx result and a message the receiver cannot process because of its own fault gets a 5xx. Because HTTP has no way to signal a bad response body, a bad RID message in a response MUST be logged and shown to the administrator. RID systems SHOULD NOT return 3xx redirections and MUST NOT follow them.
sections.eli5: If the answer is ready, the receiver hands it back right away. If not, it says 'got it, I will call you back' and later phones the sender at the same number the question came from.

sections.title: TLS Requirements and Trust
sections.content:
RID systems MUST use TLS with mutual authentication, as in RFC 2818, for confidentiality, identification and authentication. Sessions MUST use non-NULL ciphersuites for authentication, integrity and confidentiality, and may be renegotiated within those limits. A RID peer MUST NOT request, offer or use SSL 2.0, because of its known vulnerabilities.

Each consortium SHOULD use a trusted public key infrastructure (PKI) to manage identities. At a minimum, each system MUST trust a set of X.509 certificate authorities, a specific white list of X.509 subject identities, or both, and MUST verify a valid peer's fully qualified domain name or other network-layer identifier against the certificate where available. The security considerations of IODEF and RID are incorporated by reference.
sections.eli5: Both sides show ID cards before talking, and the conversation is in a code that outsiders cannot read. An old, broken kind of lock (SSL 2.0) is banned.

sections.title: The Port Assignment
sections.content: Following BCP 56 (RFC 3205), RID over HTTP/TLS is treated as a substantially new service that should be controlled at a consortium member's network border differently from ordinary HTTP/TLS. It therefore needs its own port number. IANA has assigned port 4590/tcp to RID, with the service name RID over HTTP/TLS.
sections.eli5: Because this mail is special, it gets its own door number, 4590, so guards can treat it differently from ordinary web traffic.
